$comment: Live milestone state. Version-controlled so it is auditable, and updated by the AI engineer as work lands. The Control Center reads this -- it does not guess progress.
milestone: Platform Foundation v1.0 — Enterprise Knowledge Graph live in production
phase: owned_website is LIVE in HL-BOS Core. Migration 0052 was applied to canonical production on 2026-09-10 under CEO approval: barberos.sites / site_hours / site_services / site_links, every one of them gated on barberos.is_enabled() by a trigger rather than by an application `if`, nine permission-checked functions, two new permissions, and the promotion of owned_website from 'planned' to 'available' in the same migration that gives it tables -- so the catalog has never claimed a module that did not work. It is the module all 40 analysed WNY shops point at, and it answers the audit's failing findings one for one. The apply was verified the same way as 0048-0051: a normalized fingerprint over the new tables, constraints, policies, triggers, grants, functions, enums and seed rows came back identical to the local build (a0c31416669a57cc0e7a4fd542a7f62d), and the security advisor count was unchanged at 36. Migrations 0048-0052 are now all applied; 0030 and 0031 remain applied nowhere. 1,061 pgTAP assertions, 179 edge-function tests, 796 unit tests, 0 failing. STILL NOT TRUE: no shop has a page (barberos.sites is empty in production and no tenant has the capability enabled), no page is published, no page is served anywhere -- the renderer produces HTML and nothing hosts it yet -- and no real shop website has ever been fetched.

Video Studio: a still image becomes a video, from inside the console. @hl-bos/video-studio finds the panels in a composite image by scoring every row and column for uniformity (a gutter is uniform along its length, artwork is not), plans a shot list of pans and zooms, and resolves that plan to exact rectangles at any millisecond; the Control Center's /video page records it to a real .mp4 in the browser with no account, no key and no upload. Verified end to end in headless Chromium against the CEO's own six-panel image: 6 panels found in a 3x2 grid, 8 shots, 16.7s, 1440x1416 MP4 of 7.3 MB that decodes and contains real frames. 62 unit tests. One real defect was found and fixed by that verification: the first cut cropped near-square comic panels to 16:9 and deleted the artist's caption bars, and the fix (contain-by-default framing) exposed a second bug where the renderer stretched instead of padding -- both now have regression tests that fail without the fix. Generated motion (a video model that animates the picture) is NOT built: the page names it, says what it would take, and shows no button for it.

Video Studio, second pass: the page told the CEO that generated motion needs a paid account, which is false and false in the expensive direction. Corrected: the provider panel now names the route that is genuinely our own (a freely licensed open model -- Wan, LTX -- on hardware we own, nothing metered, no image leaving our systems), states what every route costs in words about money, and is ordered cheapest-first. Status renamed needs-account -> not-built, because what is missing is the connection code, not the money. The console also now answers 'do I have an NVIDIA card?' itself, on the Video Studio page, rather than sending anyone to Device Manager -- it runs nvidia-smi, falls back to the Windows display-adapter list, distinguishes 'no card' from 'card with a missing driver', maps video memory to which models are actually runnable, and shows what it ran. The Windows branch cannot execute on the machine this was written on, so the whole decision is injectable and proved by five injected-probe tests; a mutation check confirmed they fail without the platform guard. Also fixed two shipped rendering defects found by reading the served HTML rather than the source: a sentence template that spliced a provider name into nonsense, and this toolchain dropping the space after a closing inline tag, which shipped the word 'notautomatically'.

The console can now RECEIVE work, not just send it. Until now the launcher could start the console but never update it, so once a copy of this repository was on the CEO's machine there was no way for finished work to reach him short of typing git commands -- the exact chore the operating contract forbids, and a hole left by every previous session including the one that wrote the launcher. scripts/update.mjs now runs on every start: it collects whatever has been finished since last time, reinstalls libraries if they changed, rebuilds if the code changed, then starts. It never destroys work (a folder with unsaved changes is left alone), never rewrites history (fast-forward only; a diverged folder stops and says so), never blocks startup (no network means one line and carry on), and never hangs on a credential prompt (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, so a private repo fails in seconds instead of freezing the launcher). Proved by scripts/local-test/verify-update.sh against real throwaway git repositories -- 7 git cases and 4 launcher-decision cases, all passing. One real batch defect was caught and fixed in the writing: `if A if B (X) else (Y)` binds the else to the inner if, so the first draft would have skipped the build entirely on a fresh clone and started a console that had never been built.

Shop Transformation Analysis Tool (Phase 1) + BarberOS capability spine (Phase 3). Two things the spec asked for were deliberately NOT built as specified, and both are corrections rather than shortcuts. The spec's `audit_shops` table would have been a second prospect store: visibility.prospects (migration 0017) already is 'a business the agency tenant is selling to', with the converted_tenant_id field that IS the Tool-to-BarberOS handoff, so transform_audit.shop_profiles is a satellite on it carrying only the local-business facts prospects lacks. The spec's `barberos_tenants` would have been the platform's THIRD tenant model, which the current-state audit records the cost of; a shop is a platform.tenants row and barberos.shops is a satellite. The spec also called the audit data 'tenant-agnostic', which non-negotiable #1 does not allow -- it is Herman Legacy Digital's own sales data, so it is scoped to the agency tenant, which also means a second agency can run audits later without a rewrite. The honesty rules the spec states in prose are enforced as constraints: a dimension cannot be scored 'verified' unless a finding on that run carries a real evidence URL; an 'unknown' dimension cannot carry a score and a scored one cannot be called unknown; the composite is derived and a trigger refuses to let anyone write it by hand; it is weighted only over the dimensions actually scored, and the run records how many of the possible dimensions that was so a report states its own coverage instead of implying full coverage; findings are append-only; the outreach hook must cite a finding of its own run; and a recommendation's capability_key is a foreign key, so no report can recommend a module that does not exist. On the BarberOS side, payments cannot be enabled at all (status 'deferred', refused by the enable path -- the spec's deferral made structural), the review engine's config refuses every review-gating key (non-negotiable #5, in the schema rather than in prose), and a capability cannot be enabled before its prerequisites or disabled out from under a dependent. The barbershop website rubric composes the EXISTING scanner (_shared/discovery: SSRF validation, redirect-hop checking, deterministic extraction) and adds only the barber-specific reading of those same facts. A check with nothing to judge is dropped from the denominator rather than scored zero, so a shop is never marked down for something we failed to look at. 'No website' and 'site unreachable' are kept apart: the first is a scored finding of absence at inferred confidence, the second carries no score at all and surfaces as a gap. One real defect was found by its own test and fixed: the booking detector matched the sentence 'Call 716-555-0142 to make an appointment' and scored the shop as having online booking, when that sentence describes the exact opposite. Booking now requires a CTA attached to something clickable, and a tel:/mailto: link never counts. 1,005 pgTAP assertions and 145 edge-function tests, 0 failing, run from an empty database. NOT APPLIED to any environment, no shop imported, no audit run against a real site.

Applied 0048/0049 to canonical production under CEO approval, and found two real defects doing it. FIRST: hand-transcribing the migration into the apply call changed one word of a seeded capability description ('Direct output' for 'Direct answer'). Caught by comparing production against the repo-applied local build rather than by rereading what I typed, and corrected in place. That is exactly the repo-vs-production drift ADR-0002 exists to catch, and it argues for a scripted apply path instead of a transcribed one. SECOND, and the more serious one: five format guards were written the way every HL-BOS migration writes them -- `check (key ~ '^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$')` on a citext column. That expression does not mean the same thing everywhere, because `~` is resolved from the search_path in force when the constraint is PARSED. Production's search_path includes `extensions`, so the citext operator resolves and the match is case-INSENSITIVE: 'Booking_Upper' PASSES a guard that reads as 'lowercase only'. The local sandbox's search_path does not, so the same guard is case-SENSITIVE there and the pgTAP suite proved protection production did not have. Verified by direct probe in both environments, not inferred. Migration 0050 casts the five guards explicitly -- four to text (case-sensitive, the intended lowercase-snake-case rule) and capability_requires_not_self to lower() (case-insensitive, which is the CORRECT reading for citext foreign keys onto a citext primary key, so production was right there and the sandbox was wrong). Four new pgTAP assertions test the VALUES rather than the constraint text, so they mean the same thing under either runner; a mutation check confirmed the self-requirement test accepts 'booking' requiring 'BOOKING' without the fix and refuses it with. The same shape exists on 35 further CHECK constraints across 14 other schemas, including vault-reference format guards in ai, billing, comms, integrations and social. Those are PRE-EXISTING and deployed; they are named in the session report for a separate owner decision rather than rewritten unannounced. Behaviour driven by the citext TYPE rather than by operator lookup -- unique indexes in particular -- was confirmed identical in both environments, so the import path's idempotency never diverged. Function bodies are unaffected: all 24 set search_path='' and are therefore consistently text-based in both. Post-apply state, read from production: 9 capabilities, 0 shipped, 0 enabled anywhere, 0 shops, 0 audit shops, 0 runs, 0 findings, 7 new permissions. Advisors 36 -> 36.

The analysis runner, and two more defects it exposed. _shared/transform_audit/run.ts is the piece between the rubric and the database: it owns the ORDER the schema requires (findings before the dimension score, because a dimension cannot claim 'verified' until its evidence exists; recommendations and the hook after the findings they cite). Fetching, DNS and every write are injected, so the same code runs wherever the network actually is -- the Control Center on the CEO's machine, or an edge function -- and it does not choose. Batches are sequential with a delay between shops on purpose: a burst of parallel fetches at fifty small businesses from one address is what makes a crawler look like an attack. Running it end to end for the first time found two things no unit test had. FIRST: a shop whose site refused the connection came back status 'completed'. The report underneath was honest -- coverage said 0 of 1, the finding said the site could not be read -- but a portfolio list shows the STATUS, and 'completed' next to six shops nobody managed to look at is the dashboard lying while the detail page tells the truth. Migration 0051 redefines 'completed' as every weighted dimension actually ASSESSED; a dimension recorded 'unknown' is one we could not reach, so a run carrying one is partially_completed. SECOND: report() ordered recommendations by the priority enum, whose declaration order is ('quick_win','structural'), so every report led with 'add a viewport tag' and buried 'customers cannot book you' -- inverting the analysis's own ranking and contradicting the outreach hook built from it. Now ordered structural-first explicitly, with a test whose structural row is inserted last and ranked ninth so only the explicit ordering can put it first. Proof, against the real schema and the real SQL functions with fixture pages (scripts/local-test/audit-e2e.mts): six shops audited, 70 findings, 21 recommendations, 6 dimension scores stored. Scores ran 100 (owned domain, booking, hours, prices, map, reviews) down to 17, with a booking-platform-hosted shop at 80 correctly passing booking and failing ownership, a shop with no site at 0/inferred, and an unreachable shop at no score/unknown/partially_completed. 11 new runner tests plus the existing 15 rubric tests. NOT run against a real shop website: this container's egress policy denies arbitrary hosts.

The real list, imported and analysed. 50 WNY barbershops into production under the Herman Legacy Digital tenant, every row traceable to its sheet row, and 40 complete analyses computed by the actual runner. The list drove a real correction. 40 of the 50 rows carry a research note rather than a URL, and five of those read 'Booksy presence; dedicated site not confirmed' or similar. Treating them like the other 35 would have put 'there is no way to book you online' in front of shops that are already bookable -- false, and the fastest way to lose the call. classifyWebPresence() now reads the note into three kinds, and a platform-only shop gets a DIFFERENT analysis: the missing owned domain as a failing finding, booking recorded as a PASS, no score at all (two facts from a note are not an assessment), and a hook about ownership rather than bookability. It never recommends the booking module to a shop that can already be booked. A second wording defect was caught before it reached production: the stored dimension note read '0 of 0 checks were evaluable on this page' for shops that have no page. Each no-page case now writes its own sentence, because the note is what a reader sees next to a blank score. Method: import-prospects.mts parses the workbook by header name (no new npm dependency -- it shells to openpyxl, which a one-off spreadsheet read does not justify adding a package for). The runner produced exactly 6 distinct analyses across the 40 shops, so the replay stores six templates and a row-to-template map instead of 40 copies. Both statements were dry-run against a local PostgreSQL 17.6 on the same migrations and verified by fingerprint before and after: import e895b16ca28e005f63a8428c3a31e79c, analyses 51e1c68cfcfc5dece015d027484b6ff7, identical local and production. The exact statements are kept in scripts/local-test/. Every write went through the same permission-checked SECURITY DEFINER functions a signed-in user would call; nothing was inserted around them. Documented in docs/operations/wny-barbers-50-run.md, including what this is NOT.

The Shop Analysis page, and a bug only a rendered page could show. The console now reads the campaign and every shop's full analysis out of HL-BOS Core, and can do the one thing nothing else can: open the websites of shops nobody has visited, from the machine the CEO is sitting at. The build environment's egress policy denies arbitrary hosts, so this capability could never have been delivered as a cloud job. Architecture: the page reads through the Supabase Management API's SQL endpoint using the token the console already holds -- no second credential, and no need to expose transform_audit over PostgREST, which would have meant new public RPCs and a new externally-callable surface. That endpoint connects as postgres, so every WRITE impersonates the tenant owner and goes through the same permission-checked SECURITY DEFINER functions the app uses; scripts/lib/hlbos-sql.mts owns that impersonation and refuses to run at all if the tenant has no owner to act as, rather than quietly writing as a superuser. The fetching runs as a child process, like every other slow thing the console does, one request per shop with a pause between them and an honest User-Agent. THE BUG: the shop list described five shops as "could not be read". Nobody had ever tried to read them -- they are the platform-only shops whose entire analysis came from the spreadsheet. Both cases have no score and 'unknown' confidence, so the page had collapsed two different sales situations into one false sentence. The distinction is now carried in the data (does the run have a website_unreachable finding?) rather than guessed at render time, with four tests, including one that a missing column must never be read as failure. It was found by pointing the console at a local PostgreSQL through a stand-in API and looking at fifty real shops on screen -- type checks and unit tests had all passed. That harness is kept (scripts/local-test/supabase-api-shim.cjs) so the page stays checkable. Proved: the audit script end to end against the real schema (10 shops, scores 100 down to 17, one dead site correctly recorded as unreachable with no score); the importer's write path (identical fingerprint to the earlier import, and idempotent on re-import); the page's SQL against the real schema; 48 unit tests on the mapping; the app builds and both pages render, connected and not. NOT proved: the HTTP call to the real Management API, because this environment has no Supabase token. Both runners accept either documented response shape and raise on anything else, so a wrong guess surfaces as a stated error on the page rather than as an empty list.

owned_website, the module the audit actually asks for. All 40 analysed WNY shops point at it and nothing else -- 35 with no website at all, 5 bookable only on a platform they do not own -- so it is the first BarberOS capability to come through the gate 0048 shipped empty. The gate is now load-bearing rather than advisory: barberos.require_capability() is a trigger on every table in the module, so turning the capability off does not hide a shop's page behind an `if` in an application, it makes the rows unwritable at the source. Written generically, with the capability key as a trigger argument, so every future module attaches the same function. The module maps one-for-one onto the audit's failing findings: published_hours, services_listed, pricing_published, address_or_map, tap_to_call, online_booking, social_linked. A shop fixes its audit by filling this in, and the next audit reads the new page and says so. NOTHING IS INVENTED, which is the whole design. There are no defaults for hours, prices or copy. A day with NO ROW means the shop has not said; a row with is_closed means the shop says it is closed -- the schema keeps them apart so the renderer can, because rendering silence as 'Closed' sends a customer away on a day the shop is open, and the SHOP takes that review. A null price renders 'Price on request'; a zero price is refused outright, because it would advertise a free haircut. A page cannot be PUBLISHED until it carries a headline, an address, a way to act and at least one stated day -- a blank page under a shop's own name is worse than no page. No photo gallery in v1: storage_meta.files would be the right home but nothing can upload yet, and a table nobody can fill is the empty-capability liability CONTRIBUTING warns about. THREE DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED IN THE BUILDING. (1) The publish gate appended to a text[] without a cast, so `text[] || 'a headline'` resolved to array-concat-ARRAY and raised 22P02 'malformed array literal' instead of the sentence it had carefully written. It still blocked publishing -- but a guard that fires with the wrong reason teaches whoever hits it to distrust the guard. (2) The migration claimed a manager could edit the page; 0048 had granted managers read-only. Rather than paper over it, editing page CONTENT got its own permission (barberos.site.update, granted to manager) separate from publishing (barberos.publication.manage, owner and admin only): putting this week's prices up is the daily work of running a shop, not a commercial decision. (3) The gate tests were passing on the SELECT-only grant rather than on the trigger -- same SQLSTATE, so they would have passed with no gate at all. They now run as the owner and match the trigger's own message. One test failed on purpose: 48's `t_no_capability_has_shipped_yet` asserted zero shipped modules and carried a comment saying that failing would be its job. It failed, and it was. Proved end to end against the real schema and the real permission-checked functions (scripts/local-test/barberos-site-e2e.mts): Truth Barbershop -- a real row 4 of the list, on a GlossGenius page it does not own -- gets a page with seven days of hours, five services, prices, a tap-to-call number, a map link and a booking link, published through the gate, then rendered to 4,458 bytes of HTML from what came back OUT of the database. A second shop with an empty page was refused publication, and renders as a page that says it is empty rather than a page of filler.

0052 applied to HL-BOS Core, fingerprint-verified. The gate is now load-bearing in production, not just in a test database: four capability triggers are attached, owned_website is 'available' at version 2, and it is the only capability in the catalog that is. The apply went through the Management API, which means the SQL was TRANSCRIBED rather than shipped -- ADR-0002's checksum lock does not cross that boundary, and an earlier apply in this series drifted by one word in a seed string. So the check is not 'it succeeded': the same normalized fingerprint was computed on the local mirror and on production and compared. It differed on first comparison, in exactly one component (functions). Chasing it down: all nine function bodies were byte-identical; the difference was pg_get_function_identity_arguments rendering upsert_site's citext parameter as 'citext' in production (where extensions is on the search_path) and 'extensions.citext' locally. Same type, different printing -- the same search_path-dependent citext behaviour that produced migration 0050. Normalized for that, both sides give a0c31416669a57cc0e7a4fd542a7f62d. Advisors re-run after the apply: 36 findings, the same 36 as before, none of them in barberos -- the new tables all carry policies, and the new SECURITY DEFINER functions are not in an exposed API schema. Production state confirmed by query: 10 barberos tables, 4 gate triggers, 5 barberos permissions, 1 available capability, 0 sites, 0 tenant capability rows. Nothing was written to production beyond the schema -- no shop, no page, no invented row.

blockers.title: Accounts not connected yet
blockers.meaning: Open Connect accounts in the console and paste a GitHub token and a Supabase token. Two minutes, once. Until then the console cannot show your builds or the database.

blockers.title: Deploy buttons are not built yet
blockers.meaning: Deploying needs a preview environment to test against, and Supabase branching is not switched on. Building a Deploy button before then would be a button that cannot deploy.

blockers.title: Social channels are not connected yet
blockers.meaning: The publishing software is built and tested, but it has no accounts to publish to. Six things are needed before the first real post: the exact list of Facebook Pages, Instagram accounts, LinkedIn profile and TikTok accounts to use; confirmation each Instagram account is a Professional account linked to a Facebook Page (a personal account cannot post automatically at all); a Meta app with the Instagram and Facebook Login products; a tester/admin role on that app for each account; a LinkedIn app with 'Share on LinkedIn'; and a TikTok app with inbox-only content posting. Each is an access decision only you can make. Everything not waiting on them is finished.

blockers.title: Production has drifted from the repository, and the safe apply path is blocked
blockers.meaning: While applying the social migration I checked what the live database actually contains. It holds about forty migrations that are not in this repository at all (three separate naming schemes: dma_*, disco_*, jobscout_*), and around fourteen of our own migrations were applied under different version stamps than the files carry. The registry file that is supposed to track this still says the database is at migration 28; it is far past that. The practical consequence: the protected one-click migration workflow cannot be used safely right now -- its drift check would fail, and if it were forced past that it would try to re-run around twenty migrations the database already has under other names, including two data backfills. That is why 0046 and 0047 were applied individually and verified rather than pushed as a batch. Reconciling this properly is its own piece of work and needs your go-ahead; it is not urgent, but it should not be left indefinitely.
